title: Sweetness and humility
hookLine: mitthat neevee: sweetness and humility are the essence of all virtue (Asa di Var, ang 470)

cards: An old shop scale hangs from a beam, two pans swinging under it. Put something in each pan and let go. One side rises, one side sinks.
Which side is heavier? The side that goes down. It sounds too simple to matter.

Sikh tradition remembers Guru Nanak as a young storekeeper in Sultanpur, weighing out grain on scales like this one. In the Asa di Var, he turned the old market scale into a line Sikhs still quote today.

teach.b: The salok is on ang 470. At its center are two words: mitthat and neevee. Mitthat is sweetness, from mittha, sweet, the word you'd use for sugar or a ripe mango.
Neevee is lowliness, humility, being low. Mitthat neevee Nanakaa, the line goes: sweetness and humility, Nanak, are the essence of all virtues and goodness. Not one virtue among many.
The essence. Then the salok gives the scale. Everyone bows to themselves, it says, in paraphrase; no one bows to another.

teach.h: THE SIDE THAT BENDS IS HEAVY.
teach.b: But put things on the balance and weigh them: the side that bends low is the heavy one. In the market, heavy means valuable.

teach.h: SWEET IN SPEECH, LOW IN SELF.
teach.b: So the one who bows, who stays low, is the one with real weight. Why sweetness and humility together? Think of each without the other.
Sweetness without humility can be charm: nice words that are really about being liked.

Humility without sweetness can turn sour: a person so busy feeling small that they're cold to everyone. Together, they make someone easy to be near, who doesn't need to be above you and doesn't need to hurt you.
The same salok opens with a tree and ends with a warning that bowing can be faked; we'll take both tomorrow. Some Sikhs sum up the whole path with these two words: sweet in speech, low in self.

how: Sikhs quote mitthat neevee, sweetness and humility, as a summary of Sikh character, and hear it in the dawn singing of Asa di Var.

o: a low, quiet voice in prayer

games.q: sweetness and humility — tap the pairs.
p: the heavy one on the scale

s: the salok calls sweetness and humility two virtues among many
it calls them the essence of all virtues and goodness.
on Guru Nanak's scale, the side that goes down is the heavy one
the one who bends low has the real weight.
the salok says everyone bows to others
everyone bows to themselves, it says; no one bows to another.

games.q: two pans hang on a market scale. one rises, one sinks. which one does Guru Nanak say is heavier?
games.why: everyone bows to themselves, the salok says. but on the balance, the side that bends low is the heavy one.

practice: Think of one person you tend to be short with, and find one sentence you could say to them more sweetly, softer and without the edge.
Say it in your head until it feels natural, then picture yourself lower, not smaller, just unhurried, like the heavy side of the scale. If you pray, say Waheguru.

wordCard.voice: Mitthat neevee, sweetness and lowliness: in Guru Nanak's salok, the essence of all virtue. On the scale, the side that bends low is the heavy one.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: sweetness and lowliness; mittha means sweet, neeva means low.

carryVoice: Your line: sweet and humble. On the scale, the low side is the heavy one. That's day five hundred fifty-one.

sources.ref: Asa di Var, salok M1 (simmal rukh saraaiaa ... mithat neevee Nanakaa), Ang 470
